To differentiate between substrate inhibition (M7) and catalyst-catalyst interactions (M2, M13, M18, M19), we should run an experiment with a low substrate concentration (S = 0.5) and the maximum allowable catalyst concentration (cat = 0.2), with no initial product. 
At a low substrate concentration, the formation of the inhibitory `catS2` complex in M7 will be minimized, causing M7's kinetic profile to closely resemble the standard Michaelis-Menten model (M1). Conversely, the extremely high catalyst concentration will maximize the probability of catalyst-catalyst encounters. This will strongly amplify the effects of catalyst dimerization (M2) or bimolecular catalyst deactivation (M13), leading to a distinctly reduced reaction rate or rapid early-stage deactivation compared to M1. Furthermore, this regime helps distinguish M13 (where free `cat` deactivates) from M18 (where `catS` deactivates), because the low substrate concentration limits the proportion of catalyst in the `catS` state. This orthogonal perturbation will cleanly separate the leading hypotheses based on their dependence on absolute catalyst versus substrate concentrations.
</hypothesis>
